newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Kohl celebrates German unity day in Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Kohl celebrates German unity day in Ireland.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl marked German unity day on Thursday with a speech in Dublin which said the drive towards closer European integration was both irreversible and vital for peace and prosperity.
Celebrating the day outside Germany for the first time in the six years since unification, Kohl said integration would ensure that Western Europe would never again be divided by war.
"We and our partners and friends must build a common European house, a house large enough to find room for all of those in Europe who would like to join in," Kohl said.
"It will be a house with a strict set of by-laws, a set of rules which each and every person in the house has to abide by," he told a reception to mark unity day.
"There will always be disputes and quarrels, because there will always be different interests within the European Union," Kohl said.
"But these disputes should be settled within the walls of the house in a civilised way, not on the streets as we used to do it. Settling it on the streets inevitably means war."

Kohl said the journey towards closer integration would be "fraught with risks and very exhausting", but Europe had every reason to be confident. He said he was convinced the EU would succeed in creating a successor to the Maastricht treaty within the next year, and that a single currency would go ahead.
"In 12 months we will have completed the "Mastricht two' treaty," Kohl said.
"EMU (European Monetary Union) will make progress and in spite of all the dire predictions of the pessimistic know-alls, EMU will be introduced."
Kohl said he had been asked several times why he had chosen to celebrate unity day abroad and in Ireland.
"My answer is a very clear-cut one," he said. "I wanted to use this particular day to show my sense of gratitude."
He thanked Ireland for the support it had given to German unification, and praised former Soviet president Mikhail Gorbachev and former U.S. president George Bush for their contributions.

"There were many who assisted us in achieving unification, although there were also a lot of people who were not all that enthusiastic," Kohl said. "We achieved unification with the support of our neighbours, a feat that is unparalleled in history, and we have every reason to be grateful."
Kohl arrived in Dublin on Wednesday for a two-day visit, the first official bilateral visit by a German chancellor since 1979. He last visited Ireland in 1990 to attend an EU summit.
He met Irish Prime Minister John Bruton on Wednesday for bilateral talks before addressing Ireland's parliament and attending a state banquet.
Kohl is due to return to Dublin to attend an informal summit of EU heads of state on Saturday.
